A lexicographer is a person whose job is to write, compile, or edit dictionaries.

That's the heart of it. But to truly understand this word and never forget it, let's unpack what that actually means.
What Does a Lexicographer Actually Do?

Think about the dictionary you use — whether it's a thick, heavy book on a shelf or an app on your phone. Every single word in it, every definition, every example sentence — someone had to write all of that. That someone is a lexicographer.

Their work involves:

  • Collecting words — finding words that people are actually using in real life, in books, newspapers, conversations, and online.
  • Studying how words are used — not just what a word should mean, but how real people are actually using it, in what situations, and with what tone.
  • Writing definitions — crafting clear, accurate explanations of what each word means, which is much harder than it sounds. A definition has to be precise enough to be correct, yet simple enough to be understood.
  • Finding example sentences — showing the word being used in real context, so the reader can see it in action.
  • Deciding which words make the cut — not every word that exists ends up in a dictionary. Lexicographers decide which words are used widely enough and consistently enough to deserve an entry.
  • Tracking how words change over time — words shift in meaning across decades. The word "awful" once meant worthy of awe (a good thing). A lexicographer notices and records these shifts.
  • Handling multiple meanings — many words mean different things in different contexts. A lexicographer organizes these meanings carefully and logically.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine language as a vast, wild jungle — constantly growing, changing, and expanding. New plants (words) sprout up, old ones die out, and some change their shape over time.

A lexicographer is the scientist who goes into that jungle, carefully observes everything, and then produces the official map — the dictionary — so that everyone else can navigate it.

They do not decide what the jungle should look like. They describe what it actually looks like.
An Important Distinction: They Describe, They Don't Dictate

This is a subtle but very important point. Many people assume that dictionary writers are like language judges — telling us the "correct" way to speak. In reality, a good lexicographer's job is to describe language as it is truly used, not to prescribe how it ought to be used.

So if millions of people start using the word "literally" to mean "figuratively" (as in, "I was literally on fire with excitement"), a lexicographer will eventually record that new meaning — not because they approve or disapprove of it, but because that's what the evidence of real usage shows.
The craft and study of writing dictionaries is called lexicography. So if lexicographer is the person, lexicography is the profession or discipline. A lexicographer practices lexicography.

• Samuel Johnson wrote one of the most celebrated early English dictionaries in 1755, doing much of the monumental work largely on his own.
  • Noah Webster compiled the first major American English dictionary in the early 1800s, which is why American dictionaries are still associated with his name today (Merriam-Webster).
  • James Murray was the chief editor behind the original Oxford English Dictionary — a project so enormous it took decades and hundreds of contributors to complete.

These names show you that lexicography is serious, respected, and historically significant intellectual work.
How to Remember This Word Forever

Break it down mentally (without going into formal etymology):

  • Think of "lexico" as relating to words or language (you may recognize it from words like "vocabulary").
  • Think of "grapher" as a person who writes or records something (like a photographer records images, or a cartographer maps the land).

So a lexicographer = someone who writes/records words → a dictionary writer. Simple as that.
A lexicographer is a skilled professional who researches, defines, organizes, and compiles words into a dictionary, carefully reflecting how language is genuinely used by real people.
